q: Shapiro's main complaint about how philosophers treat the multiple realizability thesis (MRT) is that:
a: They accept it too quickly, without precise criteria
w: They reject it far too quickly and without argument
It has already been disproven by experiments
They wrongly think it applies only to computers
e: They accept it too quickly, and no one has said precisely what counts as distinct realizations. Nobody has completed the sentence 'N and M are distinct realizations of T when and only when ___'.

q: Who generalized Putnam's MRT into an argument against reducing ANY special science?
w: Ned Block
Elliott Sober
John Searle
e: Fodor 'played MRT like a trump card' against reducing any science above physics.

q: Shapiro rejects Putnam's a priori argument from functional isomorphism. His mousetrap example shows that:
a: Isomorphic marks on paper aren't a mousetrap
w: Mousetraps can be multiply realized in many ways
A sheet of paper can actually catch a mouse
Isomorphism always guarantees the same kind
e: Marks on paper can be functionally isomorphic to a mousetrap without being a mousetrap. Confusing a DESCRIPTION of a system's functional relations with the system itself is the mistake.

q: Why does Shapiro call it 'curious' that Putnam's functional-isomorphism argument is a priori?
a: MRT is about physical possibility, so it's empirical
w: Putnam never actually used a priori arguments
A priori arguments in philosophy are always invalid
MRT is just true by definition of the terms
e: MRT is a thesis about physical possibility, so it should rest on empirical evidence. Whether electrical parts and cogs can both preserve a machine table's relations depends on their causal properties, which is an empirical question.

q: Shapiro reconstructs Putnam's argument for MRT as a likelihood argument. What's the evidence MR makes more probable than type identity?
w: Humans having C-fibers
Computers passing the Turing Test
Brains being made of neurons
e: Mammals, reptiles, mollusks and aliens all sharing a psychological state like pain. Like the Rounders poker example: the same faces winning every year is more likely if poker takes skill.

q: Shapiro's 'scratchers of sapphires' example makes what point?
a: A kind could have only one physical realizer
w: All kinds whatsoever are multiply realizable
Sapphires are actually harder than diamonds
Hardness turns out to be a mental property
e: A kind could, as an empirical matter, have just one physically possible realizer (diamond). MRT is empirical and could turn out false for minds. Putnam even notes octopus and mammal eyes evolved nearly identical structures.

q: Which is NOT one of Block and Fodor's empirical considerations for MRT?
w: Convergent evolution
Neural plasticity (Lashleyan equipotentiality)
The conceptual possibility of machine minds
e: Amusingly, they cite convergent evolution, the same phenomenon Putnam took as the best reason to DOUBT MRT.

q: Why isn't water a candidate for multiple realizability, per Shapiro?
a: It's defined by its structure, not its function
w: It is far too common in nature to count
It's a mental kind rather than a physical kind
It could be made of anything at all, so it's trivial
e: It's defined by molecular structure (H2O), not by what it does. MRT can only be true of kinds defined by purpose, capacity, or contribution to an end, like carburetors and minds.

q: Are a steel waiter's corkscrew and an aluminum waiter's corkscrew different realizations of a corkscrew?
a: No, rigidity screens off the material
w: Yes, different metals mean different realizations
Yes, but only if they are painted different colors
No, because aluminum can't remove corks
e: No: they share the causally relevant property (rigidity), which screens off the material difference. Their difference is no more relevant than a yellow vs. red corkscrew.

q: Which pair DOES count as genuinely different realizations of a corkscrew?
a: A lever corkscrew and a winged corkscrew
w: A red and a yellow waiter's corkscrew
A steel and an aluminum waiter's corkscrew
Two identical winged corkscrews
e: A waiter's corkscrew (lever) and a winged corkscrew (rack and pinion). They use different mechanisms, described by different laws. They differ in causally relevant properties.

q: Shapiro's key criterion: realizations are truly multiple only when they differ in:
w: Their color or surface finish
Their physical composition
The name we happen to give them
e: Causally relevant properties: those that affect how they contribute to the defining capacity. Mere differences in constitution aren't enough.

q: On Shapiro's view, a brain with every neuron replaced by a functionally identical silicon chip is:
w: Obviously a distinct realization
Not a brain at all
Proof of dualism
e: Not a distinct realization, if the chips contribute in exactly the same causal way. The difference would be no more interesting than gray neurons vs. purple-stained neurons.

q: Shapiro agrees with Putnam that octopus and mammal eyes are NOT different realizations, but suggests which ARE?
w: Octopus eyes and squid eyes
Left and right human eyes
Blue eyes and brown eyes
e: Camera eyes and compound eyes (as in arthropods). Camera and compound eyes 'do the same thing' in very different ways, with different optical principles.

q: Shapiro's dilemma for MRT: if realizers don't differ in causally relevant properties, it's not MR. If they do differ:
a: They share no interesting laws, so aren't one kind
w: They turn out to be type-identical after all
They must all be made of the same material
They can no longer perform the same function
e: There are no interesting laws common to them, so they don't form a single scientific kind. The only 'law' about all eyes would be analytic and dull: all eyes have the function to see.

q: Shapiro says macrolevel laws about water (viscosity, freezing point) are possible because:
a: The same micro laws hold for all water
w: Water can be realized in many ways
Water is defined as a functional kind
Laws about water are true by definition
e: The same microlevel laws hold for all samples of water. Micro laws determine macro laws. Functional kinds with different micro mechanisms lack this unifying basis.

q: In Shapiro's Figure 2, aquatic camera eyes all have graded spherical lenses. This shows that:
a: Higher-level laws can reduce to lower-level ones
w: Reduction would destroy the science of vision
Eyes aren't real, only their parts are
Optics is just another special science
e: Higher-level laws (anatomy) can reduce to lower-level laws (optics), which helps the special sciences. Which proteins make up the lens doesn't matter. The refractive gradient screens off protein composition.

q: What does Shapiro conclude is the real value of functional kinds (like 'eye') in the special sciences?
a: Comparing them reveals causally relevant properties
w: They enter into rich and interesting empirical laws
They prove that reduction is always impossible
They have no real value in science at all
e: They group phenomena so comparisons reveal which properties are causally relevant. The special sciences should aim to understand HOW functional kinds produce their capacities, not to find laws over functional kinds.
